summary:
LA-IRA (LunarAres - Integrated Route Assistant) is an offline-capable EVA planning and navigation web tool for Martian astronauts exploring Gale Crater.

It translates raw NASA planetary data for field safety by combining high-resolution mapping, mineral targets, thermal sand masks, and radiation estimates. The system computes optimal, terrain-aware walking routes and dynamic timelines using an advanced A* pathfinding algorithm.

On Mars, improper route planning or unexpected hazards can put an astronaut's life at risk. A-IRA provides real-time, self-contained decision support in the field without needing cloud connectivity, maximizing both scientific discovery and crew safety during complex surface explorations.
details:
LA-IRA (LunarAres – Integrated Route Assistant) is an Extravehicular Activity (EVA) route-planning web tool built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It currently maps two target sites: a 2.46 × 2.46 km region around the Mount Sharp boxwork formations in Gale Crater on Mars (explored by Curiosity), and the Apollo 17 landing site in the Taurus-Littrow valley on the Moon.

The application runs on a modular data pipeline and a two-stage interface:

  1. Source Verification & Startup Gate: When you select a celestial body on startup, the app runs live health checks (OK / FAIL) against each configured NASA endpoint. You can toggle which data layers feed into the planner or plug in a custom ArcGIS ImageServer or WMTS URL. Only topography is strictly required—if optional layers are disabled or an endpoint goes down, the planner falls back and continues with the available data.
    • Topography & Slope (HiRISE 1 m DTM / LROC NAC 5 m DTM): Calculates terrain gradients using the Horn method (3×3 window), blocking cells that exceed maximum forward or cross-slope limits and adding a cost penalty to caution slopes (greater than 15°).
    • Optical Imagery & Relief: Stitches 15×15 WMTS tiles from the HiRISE (~0.6 m/px) or LROC NAC mosaics into a 3840×3840 base map, layered with a server-rendered DTM hillshade.
    • Thermal Sand Proxy (THEMIS Night IR, ~100 m/px): Flags the coldest 30% of the region at night—where low thermal inertia indicates loose sand and dust—and applies an adjustable walking-time penalty.
    • Mineralogy & Target Suggestions (CRISM MTRDR, 18 m/px): Georeferences CRISM spectral browse products (sulfates, clays, carbonates, and true color) using PDS3 labels, then automatically picks up to 6 scientific points of interest based on the strongest sulfate signals located on walkable slopes.
    • Sky-View Radiation Estimate (Curiosity RAD / LRO CRaTER + DTM): Pulls a reference dose rate—including live HTTP Range reads of the latest 5 sols from the ~70 MB/sol Curiosity RAD archive paired with recent MSL waypoints—and scales it by the visible sky fraction (cos⁡2\cos^2cos2 of the horizon angle across 16 directions out to ~390 m). This highlights where surrounding topography provides natural radiation shielding.
    • Pathfinding & Emergency Return Map: Estimates walking speed with an adapted Tobler function and computes paths using A*, Dijkstra, or D* Lite. It optimizes stop order (caching previously solved legs so only modified segments are recalculated) and runs a reversed Dijkstra search from the Habitat to map 30-, 60-, and 90-minute emergency return boundaries across the map.

What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact?

  • EVA Safety & Life-Support Budgeting: Astronauts and mission planners can immediately track total travel time, science time per stop, worst-case return time to the habitat, cumulative elevation gain/loss, sand traversal distance, and estimated radiation exposure (µGy) against suit limits and safety reserves.
  • Offline Reliability: Once loaded, the app works fully offline by caching terrain packages in the browser's IndexedDB and verifying data integrity with SHA-256 hashes. In live Vercel deployments, it queries NASA endpoints on demand and automatically falls back to packaged snapshots if any external service is unreachable.
  • Easy Expansion to New Sites: Any planetary region can be added without changing core code by supplying a JSON body profile or a Schema 1 data package (meta.json + base64 float32 elev.txt).

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: Vanilla JavaScript (ES Modules), HTML5 (using <canvas> for dynamic layer rendering, pixel extraction, and elevation profiles), CSS3, and Leaflet 1.9.4 (EPSG:4326), built with zero bundlers or build steps.
  • Backend & Data Pipeline: Python 3.12 (managed with uv), using Pillow (PIL) and requests for WMTS tile stitching, ArcGIS ImageServer float32 DEM exports, PDS3 label parsing, and HTTP Range requests.
  • Deployment & Testing: Vercel (Python serverless functions in api/), Node.js built-in test runner (node:test), and Python unittest.
  • NASA Data Sources: NASA Mars Trek, NASA Moon Trek, NASA Planetary Data System (PDS Geosciences & PPI), HiRISE, CRISM, THEMIS, MSL Curiosity RAD & MMGIS waypoints, and LRO LROC & CRaTER.

How is your project creative and what factors did your team consider?

  • Targeted HTTP Range Reads for Live Radiation Data: Rather than downloading massive ~70 MB PDS tables in full, the backend uses byte-range requests to fetch only the latest Curiosity RAD measurements, combining them with a DTM-based horizon model to map terrain radiation shelter in real time.
  • Asymmetric Reversed Dijkstra Return Map: Because walking uphill and downhill have different Tobler speeds and slope limits, simply reversing a forward path gives the wrong return time. Our emergency return map reverses edge directions (v→uv \to uv→u) when expanding outward from the habitat, showing the actual time needed to get back to safety from any point on the grid.
  • Suit Mobility Constraints: The pathfinding model accounts for both forward slope and sideways cross-slope limits, slowdowns in loose sand, and an equipment-carrying mode that tightens slope limits by 5° and reduces walking speed by 20%.
  • Transparent Model Limitations: Because planetary datasets vary widely in scale, the UI explicitly displays the resolution and constraints of every active layer—noting, for example, that ~2.4 m cells cannot resolve meter-scale boulders, CRISM alignment is approximate at ~18 m/px, THEMIS night IR is a ~100 m regional heuristic, and Tobler's function is an Earth-derived hiking model. Missing data is always flagged as unavailable rather than silently defaulted to zero.
